title: 6.32.2 Check: the Checkers game
description: Five multiple-choice questions on dark squares, the halfway square, kings and toLowerCase, crowning in a chain, and checking a move in onMove. Checked instantly.

questions.question: A square is dark when (r + c) % 2 === 1. Which of these squares is dark?
options: Row 0, column 0
Row 2, column 5
Row 3, column 3
Row 4, column 6
questions.explanation: 2 + 5 is 7, which is odd, so 7 % 2 is 1. The other three add up to an even number.

questions.question: A red piece jumps from row 5, column 2 to row 3, column 4. Which square holds the piece it jumps over?
options: Row 4, column 3
Row 3, column 3
Row 4, column 2
Row 5, column 4
questions.explanation: The halfway square is ((5 + 3) / 2, (2 + 4) / 2), which is row 4, column 3.

questions.question: Once there are kings, why does colorOf(p) return p.toLowerCase()?
options: So that a red king 'R' still counts as a red piece
So that the letters on the board are easier for the players to read
So that a king can never be jumped over by the other side
So that every piece is crowned as soon as it reaches row 0
questions.explanation: Every rule asks whether colorOf(p) === turn, and turn is 'r' or 'b'. 'R'.toLowerCase() is 'r', so a king is still its own side's piece.

questions.question: Red jumps onto row 0 and is crowned. From that square it could jump again. What happens next?
options: It must jump again before the turn passes
Crowning ends the turn, so it is black's turn
The new king is taken off the board at once
Red wins the game straight away, as it has a king
questions.explanation: doMove asks canJumpFrom only when nothing was crowned, so a crowning ends the chain and the turn passes.

questions.question: Online, why does onMove call isLegal before it calls doMove?
options: To make the move happen faster on the other computer
So both computers ignore the same bad moves and stay alike
Because doMove cannot run unless the room is still open
So that a player can take back a move they did not want to make
questions.explanation: Both computers run the same rule check on the same list of moves, so a broken or out-of-turn move is ignored everywhere and the boards still agree.
